PAX only affects layout inside pages; it does not affect I/O behavior

at.deep: Why the page is the unit that matters

items.item: Parquet is a column-oriented file format for efficient storage and retrieval
Parquet allows compression and encoding to be specified per column
NSM (row-major, slotted-page) storage makes a single-row point lookup one contiguous read, because every attribute of a row sits together.
The same row-major layout has no way to skip attributes it doesn't need during a column scan, so a scan still touches every byte of every row.

at.step: Reveal: the scan row storage cannot avoid

items.item: DSM (full column decomposition) makes a column scan touch only that column's own storage, but a point lookup now costs one read per attribute plus a join to reconstruct the row.

at.step: Reveal: DSM wins the scan, loses the lookup

items.item: PAX keeps a row's attributes on one page (like NSM) but groups each attribute's values into a per-page minipage, so a point lookup still touches one page while a scan can skip straight to the minipage it needs.

PAX's own design claim is that it changes layout inside a page only, not which pages are read: a column scan under PAX opens exactly as many pages as NSM would, with a much higher useful-byte fraction per page.

Parquet is the real-world payoff of this compromise: a column-oriented file format whose compression and encoding are tunable per column, which only makes sense once that column's values are already grouped together.

None of these three layouts is universally "better"; the right choice tracks the access pattern (point lookups and writes vs. scans) this topic measures directly, which is the same OLTP-vs-OLAP distinction Chapter 3 introduced.

at.deep: Why the page is the unit that matters

items.item: The Decomposition Storage Model (DSM) predates its modern columnar descendants by over a decade (proposed 1985, per the PAX paper's own citation); this topic measures its trade-off directly rather than treating "columnar" as a single undifferentiated idea.

at.step: Reveal: DSM wins the scan, loses the lookup

items.item: A page remains the fixed unit of I/O across all three layouts in this topic; what changes between NSM, DSM and PAX is never how large a page is, but how values are arranged inside it (NSM, PAX) or whether attributes share a page at all (DSM).

at.deep: Why the page is the unit that matters

items.item: This topic's own byte-touched numbers (32 bytes/1 read, 32,000 bytes, 4 reads, 8,000 bytes, 1 page, 10 pages, 25%) are a sandbox's deterministic measurement on a 1,000-row, 4-attribute table — a worked illustration of the trade-off, not a claim about any production system's exact numbers.
